title: Adaptive tiling & memory planner for FlashAttn v3 (v2 compatibility)
creator: Maya Chen
description: Background: We have intermittent regressions when enabling FlashAttention v3 kernels for long-prefill batches and variable token shapes. Some sequences (long context + large batch) trigger higher memory variance that causes the scheduler to fall back to suboptimal kernels or OOMs during decode. This ticket implements a runtime memory planner + adaptive tiling layer that: (1) predicts token-memory curves for a request, (2) chooses v3 vs v2 kernels based on real-time memory headroom and performance model, and (3) provides controlled fallbacks with warm-prefetch of KV/tiles to avoid tail latency spikes. Goal: eliminate regressions observed in nightly perf tests for v3 while keeping the v3 throughput/latency advantages for the common case.
acceptance_criteria: Nightly benchmark: no regressions vs baseline v2 for 99th-percentile latency on prefill+decode scenarios (within 5% of v2) for target models (llama-3-70b and rw-30b),
Memory safety: zero OOM incidents across stress job fleet (prefill lengths up to 32k tokens, batch sizes up to 16) for 72-hour soak run
Throughput preservation: average tokens/sec for typical workloads must be >= 95% of current FlashAttn v3 runs where v3 previously improved throughput
Telemetry: new metrics published (kernel_choice_reason, predicted_mem_peak, actual_mem_peak, fallback_count) and dashboards wired into Console runtime-1.20 board
Automated regression alert: evaluation suite triggers a signal in Slack and attaches perf snapshot when avg >10% deviation for 3 consecutive runs
implementation_steps: Design memory model: collect per-layer per-seqlen memory curves from profiler and fit small lookup table + interpolation (ENG-25341-M1)
Tiling planner: implement a lightweight tiler that splits attention matmul into tiles when memory headroom low and selects optimal tiling factor for v3 kernels
Kernel compatibility shim: add a decision function that returns (kernel_variant, tiling_plan, prefetch_instructions) per request; ensure deterministic fallback order: v3->v2->compat_fallback
Scheduler integration: surface predicted_mem_peak to the prefill/decode scheduler and add a soft backpressure signal to reduce batch size when necessary
Prefetch & warmup: implement async prefetch of KV tiles for chosen tiling plan to reduce first-token latency on decode
Expose flags: runtime flags for forced-v2, force-tiling, and a safety-mode to limit v3 usage for canary customers
Metrics & tracing: instrument kernel decision path and record predicted vs observed memory and latency per request
testing_plan: Unit tests: tiling planner correctness on synthetic shapes and stochastic validation against brute-force allocator
Integration tests: end-to-end prefill+decode on CI with small GPU instance; run across seqlen {512,2048,4096,8192,16384} and batch sizes {1,4,8,16}
Soak tests: 72-hour fleet soak in staging with traffic replay from production traces (long-tail contexts enabled)
A/B canary: route 5% traffic to runtime-1.20 canary with adaptive planner enabled and monitor key metrics (99p latency, OOMs, throughput)
Benchmark suite: run nightly perf job and compare to baseline artifacts; fail PRs that regress >5% in median throughput for controlled inputs
rollout_plan: Feature branch -> internal PR with unit/integration tests
Staging deploy with metrics collection and 72h soak
Canary: enable for small percentage of customers with safety-mode true
Gradual ramp: 5% -> 25% -> 60% -> 100% over 2 weeks conditioned on no alerts
Final: flip default v3 enablement for runtime-1.20 and deprecate forced-v2 flag after 4 weeks
risks: Model mismatch: memory model may mispredict pathological shapes (sparse/uneven attention masks) leading to unexpected OOMs
Latency spikes from prefetch: async prefetch increases memory footprint temporarily and may cause transient GC/backpressure
Complexity: additional decision logic increases surface area for bugs and hard-to-reproduce scheduling interactions
Operational: dashboards/alerts not wired correctly could allow regressions to reach customers
